title: εἰμί and the simplest sentences

objectives.can: Parse the present and imperfect indicative of εἰμί.
Read a sentence with εἰμί, finding its subject and predicate, including where the verb is left out.

explanation.summary: εἰμί, 'I am', is the commonest verb in the New Testament and the simplest: it links a subject to what is said about it. Learning its present and imperfect forms gives you your first complete sentences, and your first sentences with no verb written at all.

sections.heading: The forms of εἰμί
body: εἰμί has irregular forms, and you should learn them as they are. The present indicative is εἰμί, εἶ, ἐστίν, ἐσμέν, ἐστέ, εἰσίν: 'I am, you are, he/she/it is, we are, you are, they are'. The imperfect, the ordinary Greek past tense of εἰμί, is ἤμην, ἦς, ἦν, ἦμεν, ἦτε, ἦσαν: 'I was, you were, he/she/it was, we were, you were, they were'. The tables below are filled in from the New Testament and the other texts; a dash means that the form is not found in them.

The person and number are in the ending, as with every Greek verb, so the pronoun is not needed: ἐστέ alone means 'you (plural) are'. A pronoun is added for emphasis or contrast, as in Ἐγώ εἰμι in John 8:12 and Ὑμεῖς ἐστε in Matthew 5:14.

Most present forms are enclitic: they lean on the word before them and usually lose their own accent. This is why you meet both ἐστιν and ἐστίν, and also ἔστιν; the placing of the accent follows the rules for such words. When a form like ἔστιν is accented, it often means 'there is' or 'it is possible', but you will do best to read the sense from the sentence. εἶ ('you are') is not enclitic.

sections.heading: Subject and predicate
body: With εἰμί the verb does not do anything to an object. It joins a subject to a predicate: a noun, an adjective or a pronoun that says who or what the subject is. Both are in the nominative, so the case does not tell you which is which. In Matthew 5:14, Ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου, ὑμεῖς (nominative) is the subject and τὸ φῶς is the predicate: 'you are the light of the world'. The predicate is called a predicate nominative.

To find the subject, use these clues in this order. First, the verb ending: ἐστέ is 'you (plural)', so ὑμεῖς, not φῶς, is the subject. Second, a pronoun is nearly always the subject if one is present. Third, a noun with the article is usually the subject, and a noun without it is usually the predicate. This last point is a tendency, not a law. In 1 John 4:8, ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν, ὁ θεός has the article and ἀγάπη has not: 'God is love'. The words cannot be turned round: ἀγάπη is the predicate.

When both have the article, or neither, the context decides. In John 1:4, ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, both ζωή and φῶς have the article. The clause picks up ζωή from the clause before it, so ἡ ζωή is the subject.

sections.heading: Predicate adjectives and word order
body: A predicate can also be an adjective, which agrees with the subject in case, number and gender. In John 4:19, προφήτης εἶ σύ has the predicate noun first and the pronoun last. In 1 John 3:2, νῦν τέκνα θεοῦ ἐσμεν: τέκνα is nominative plural, the predicate, and the subject is 'we', carried by the ending of ἐσμεν. Greek word order is free and is used for emphasis, so never decide the subject by the order of words alone.

In John 1:1, θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, the predicate θεός comes first and has no article, and the subject ὁ λόγος has the article and comes last. The article marks ὁ λόγος as the subject. How best to put the sense of a predicate like this into English is a matter on which grammarians differ; this lesson only shows how the clause is built.

sections.heading: The verb that is not written
body: Greek often leaves out a present form of εἰμί, especially in short statements, sayings and answers. You read such a sentence by supplying 'is' or 'are', in the person and number of the subject. In John 4:24, πνεῦμα ὁ θεός has no verb: the subject is ὁ θεός and the predicate is πνεῦμα. In John 15:5, ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος, ὑμεῖς τὰ κλήματα, the second clause has no verb and the sense is 'you are the branches'. In Romans 7:12, ὁ νόμος ἅγιος is the same: 'the law is holy'. In Matthew 5:3, Μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι is a sentence with no verb, though the next clause has ἐστιν.

sections.heading: Little words that build sentences
body: Five small words are in nearly every sentence. καί means 'and', 'also' or 'even'. δέ is a mild 'but', 'and' or 'now': it joins a sentence to what went before and usually stands second in its clause, never first. οὐ means 'not'; before a vowel with a smooth breathing it is οὐκ, and before a rough breathing it is οὐχ. ἀλλά means 'but' and marks a stronger contrast than δέ; before a vowel it is elided to ἀλλ’. ὅτι introduces a clause and means 'that' or 'because'.

John 1:8 has several together: οὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖνος τὸ φῶς, ἀλλ’ ἵνα μαρτυρήσῃ περὶ τοῦ φωτός. οὐκ negates ἦν, and ἀλλ’ turns the sentence round: 'he was not the light, but …'. In John 4:19, ὅτι introduces what the woman perceives, 'that you are a prophet'.

misunderstandings: The first noun in a sentence with εἰμί is not automatically the subject. Look for the article, for a pronoun and for the person of the verb.
A sentence with no verb is not broken. It is a complete clause in which a form of εἰμί, usually the present, has been left unwritten.
ἦν is not 'is': it is the imperfect, 'was'. In the third person singular it looks like nothing else you have met, so learn it by itself.
The accent on ἐστίν, ἐστιν and ἔστιν does not make three different words. It is the same verb; the accent is a matter of the rules for enclitics.
A predicate noun is not an object. It is in the nominative, because it is not acted on.

deeper.heading: Why the predicate often has no article
body: The tendency for a predicate noun to lack the article, especially when it stands before the verb, has been studied since E. C. Colwell drew attention to it in the 1930s. Scholars disagree about how to describe the result in English: some say that the predicate states a quality or class, others that it names something definite. For reading, it is enough to notice the pattern and use it to find the subject.

examples.analysis: θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. ἦν is the imperfect, third person singular. ὁ λόγος has the article and is the subject; θεός has none and is the predicate, although it comes first. Both are nominative singular masculine, so the article, not the case, shows which is which.

Subject ἐκεῖνος, predicate τὸ φῶς; οὐκ negates ἦν
Subject ἦν, predicate τὸ φῶς; οὐκ is a conjunction
check.explain: A demonstrative pronoun such as ἐκεῖνος is a subject, and τὸ φῶς is the predicate. οὐκ is the negative 'not' (οὐ before a smooth breathing), and it stands before the verb it negates.

options: ἡ βασιλεία: nominative with the article
check.explain: αὐτῶν is genitive, so it cannot be the subject; it is the predicate, 'theirs'. ἡ βασιλεία is nominative and has the article.

check.prompt: In προφήτης εἶ σύ (words 7 to 9), which is the predicate, and why is εἶ second person?

Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: σύ is the predicate; εἶ is third person
προφήτης is the predicate; εἶ is second person singular, agreeing with σύ
προφήτης is the subject because it comes first
προφήτης is the object of εἶ
check.explain: εἶ is the second person singular, and its subject is the pronoun σύ. προφήτης, without the article, is a predicate noun, even though it comes first.

check.prompt: In νῦν τέκνα θεοῦ ἐσμεν (words 1 to 4), what is the subject?

quoted.title: 1 John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: 'We', contained in the ending of ἐσμεν
θεοῦ, because it is a person
check.explain: ἐσμεν is first person plural. No pronoun is written, so the subject is in the ending. τέκνα is the predicate; θεοῦ is a genitive of the noun τέκνα: 'children of God'.

options: ὁ θεός: it has the article
check.explain: The subject ὁ θεός has the article. φῶς has none and is the predicate. ἐστιν only joins them.

check.prompt: In ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα (words 11 to 14), why is εἰμι first person singular?

options: Its subject is the pronoun ἐγώ
check.explain: The verb takes its person and number from its subject, ἐγώ. ἡ θύρα is the predicate, and its gender does not change the verb. Compare the second person plural ἐστε in the last verse.

check.prompt: Both ζωή and φῶς have the article in ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς (words 5 to 9). Which is the subject?

options: Neither: the sentence has two subjects
ἡ ζωή: it takes up the ζωή of the previous clause
check.explain: When both have the article, the context decides. The clause before it (ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν) is about life, so ἡ ζωή is the subject here.

check.prompt: What does ἀλλ’ (word 5) do in this verse?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: It is ἀλλά, 'but', elided: it sets the point against the negative before it
check.explain: ἀλλά is a strong 'but'. After a negative (οὐκ ἦν …) it often introduces what is true instead. The vowel is dropped before ἵνα.

reading.why: The opening of John is built from the verb εἰμί: ἦν, subjects with and without the article, and predicates before the verb, together with καί, οὐκ and ἀλλ’.
